AAXJ: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies across Asia outside Japan, such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, following an MSCI index. Chip makers stand out: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix together are about 30% of the fund.
ACWI: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed and emerging markets around the world, following an MSCI index and weighted by size. US companies are the biggest share, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 12% of it.
ACWX: Stocks from nearly every country in the world except the US, covering both developed and emerging markets, tracking the MSCI ACWI ex USA index. Financials and technology lead, and Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and ASML are the biggest names at roughly 5% or less each.
AGG: A broad bundle of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, tracking an index of the total US investment-grade bond market. It is a common core bond holding: thousands of bonds, none more than a sliver, paying income through interest.
AIA: The 50 largest companies from Asia outside Japan, mainly China, Taiwan, South Korea and India, weighted by company size. It is heavily tied to chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung alone are about 40% of the fund.
AIQ: Global companies involved in artificial intelligence and big data, picked by a Global X index. It is chunky in memory chips: SK Hynix, Micron, AMD and Samsung together are about 22% of the fund, and about 70% sits in technology.
AIRR: Small and mid-sized US industrial companies, such as builders, engineers and logistics firms, picked by a First Trust index that favors firms with strong results. It is concentrated, with the top few holdings around 4% to 6% each.
AKRE: An actively managed fund holding a small number of businesses Akre Capital believes can compound their profits for years. It is very concentrated: Mastercard and Constellation Software together are about 27% of it, and it holds some non-US companies too.
AMLP: Pipeline and energy storage businesses structured as master limited partnerships, tracking the Alerian MLP Infrastructure Index. It is concentrated, with the top four holdings each around 13%, and is known mainly for the income these companies pay out.
AOR: A ready-made mix of roughly 60% stocks and 40% bonds, built by holding other iShares funds instead of individual securities. The S&P 500 fund alone is about a third of it, and the rest is spread over international stocks and bonds.
ARKK: An actively managed fund from ARK that bets on companies it thinks will be changed by new technology, like genetics, AI, robotics and online platforms. It is concentrated and volatile: Tesla is about 10% of it and the top holdings are roughly a third.
ARTY: Companies tied to artificial intelligence, such as chip designers, memory makers and software firms, from the US and abroad, picked by an index. It is a theme fund with a lot of chip stocks, and the top holdings like Micron, AMD and Taiwan Semiconductor are each about 5%.
AVDE: Companies of all sizes from developed countries outside the US, picked by Avantis with a tilt toward cheaper and more profitable stocks. It is actively run and very diversified, with ASML, Roche, Shell and HSBC each around 1% or less.
AVDV: Small companies from developed countries outside the US that look cheap relative to their book value, with Avantis also screening for profitability. It is actively run and spread across many countries and hundreds of stocks, with no holding above about 2%.
AVEM: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks, such as Taiwan, China, India and South Korea, picked by Avantis with a tilt toward cheaper, more profitable companies. It holds thousands of stocks, with SK Hynix, Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung about 20% of it.
AVLV: Large US companies that look cheap relative to their book value, with Avantis also screening for profitability. It is actively run and rules-based, not an index tracker, and Micron, Amazon, Apple and Meta are among its biggest holdings.
AVUS: US companies of all sizes, with extra weight on smaller, cheaper and more profitable stocks than the overall market, picked by Avantis' rules rather than an index. Still tech-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 15% of the fund.
AVUV: An actively managed fund of small US companies that look cheap and are more profitable, picked by Avantis using its own screens rather than a standard index. It holds hundreds of stocks with none above about 1.5%, and leans toward financials, consumer companies and energy.
BAI: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies tied to artificial intelligence, including chip makers and other technology firms in the US and abroad. It is concentrated in tech, about 90% of it, with Micron, AMD, NVIDIA and Taiwan Semiconductor leading at roughly 5% each.
BBAX: Large and mid-size companies from Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand, which is developed Asia Pacific without Japan. Financials are almost half, and BHP and Commonwealth Bank of Australia are each about 9 to 10% of the fund.
BBCA: Canadian stocks traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange, weighted by company size. Banks lead: Royal Bank, TD and Bank of Montreal, plus Shopify, make up about 25% of the fund.
BBEU: A low cost fund that holds large and mid-sized companies across developed Europe, including the UK, France, Germany and Switzerland, tracked by an index. ASML is about 5% of it, and financials and industrials are the biggest areas.
BBIN: Large and mid-size companies from developed countries outside the US, such as Europe, Japan, Canada and Australia, weighted by market size. It is fairly spread out, with ASML at about 3% the biggest, and leans toward financials, industrials, technology and health care.
BBJP: Large and mid-sized Japanese companies, tracking a market-weighted index of stocks on the Tokyo exchange. It is a low-cost way to hold Japan, and Mitsubishi UFJ, Toyota, Sumitomo Mitsui and Hitachi are among the biggest holdings, each about 3% to 5%.
BBUS: A low cost fund that holds roughly the largest 85% of the US stock market by value, mostly large and mid-sized companies. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it, so it behaves much like a broad US market index.
BCI: A broad bundle of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, tracked through futures contracts on the Bloomberg Commodity Index rather than physical goods. The fund holds Treasury bills as backing for those contracts.
BIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in one to three months, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
BILS: US Treasury bills that mature in 3 to 12 months, following a Bloomberg index. The bills are so short that the price barely moves, and the income it pays tracks short-term interest rates.
BINC: An actively managed bond fund that mixes high-yield corporate bonds, government debt and other loans, with managers choosing across the bond market rather than following an index. It is built for income and can shift between sectors as managers see fit.
BIV: A mix of US government bonds and investment grade company bonds that mature in five to ten years, weighted by size, following a Bloomberg index. It sits in the middle on risk among bond funds: more price movement than short bonds, less than long ones.
BKLC: Roughly the 500 largest US companies, following a large-company US index weighted by company size. It works like a plain S&P 500 fund and is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of it, and technology is around 40%.
BKLN: Senior loans, which are loans made by banks to companies with weaker credit ratings, that rank first in line for repayment. Their interest rates float with short-term rates, and the fund spreads across many borrowers, each under about 2%.
BLCR: An actively managed fund from BlackRock that picks large US companies using a mix of computer models and analyst research, instead of following an index. NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet together are about 30% of it.
BLV: US government and investment grade corporate bonds that mature in more than 10 years, tracked by a Bloomberg index. Long bonds pay more income but their prices move a lot when interest rates change, and the Treasuries are many small slices of about 1%.
BND: One fund holding a broad mix of US investment-grade bonds: Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It spreads across thousands of bonds, so no single one is more than a sliver, and it earns its return mostly from interest.
BNDX: Investment-grade bonds issued by governments and companies outside the US, with currency swings hedged back to US dollars. The hedge means returns follow the bonds rather than exchange rates, and holdings include UK gilts and French government bonds.
BOND: An actively managed bond fund from PIMCO, mainly investment grade bonds such as US Treasuries and mortgage bonds, with managers choosing what to hold. It can also use derivatives, which are contracts that track other assets, so it is more flexible than a plain index fund.
BOXX: A fund built around box spreads, which are paired options contracts on the S&P 500 that behave like a short-term loan. It aims to act like a very short-term Treasury bill, with a steady price and returns that follow short-term interest rates.
BSCR: A basket of US investment grade company bonds that all mature in 2027. As bonds mature, the fund steadily winds down and then closes at the end of 2027, so it behaves a bit like a single bond, with spread out holdings from big banks and tech companies.
BSCS: A basket of investment-grade US company bonds that all mature in 2028. The fund shuts down around the end of 2028 and hands back what is left, and no single company is more than about 1%.
BSV: US government and investment-grade corporate bonds maturing in 1 to 5 years, weighted by size. The short maturities mean it moves less when interest rates change than longer-term bond funds, and US Treasuries are its largest holdings.
BTC: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its price, so shares let you get bitcoin exposure through a regular brokerage account without owning it directly. It holds nothing but bitcoin, so it moves with the price of one volatile digital asset.
BUFR: A fund that holds 12 other First Trust buffer funds, each using options to limit S&P 500 losses up to a set level over a year in exchange for a cap on gains. Their start dates are staggered, and it holds nothing else.
CALF: US small companies that generate lots of free cash flow, meaning cash left after running the business, relative to their stock price. It is evenly spread, with no holding above about 3%.
CGBL: A manager-run mix of roughly 60% stocks and 36% bonds in one fund, with the bond part held through two Capital Group bond ETFs. It spreads across sectors, with technology the biggest at about 32%, and the manager shifts the stock and bond mix within set ranges.
CGCB: A manager-run fund of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, aiming for steady income and protecting capital. It is spread across many issues, with no single bond above about 1.3%.
CGCP: An actively managed bond fund from Capital Group holding US Treasuries, mortgage bonds, corporate bonds and some higher risk debt. The managers choose the bonds instead of following an index, aiming for income with a broad mix.
CGDG: An actively managed global fund of large companies that the manager expects to pay and grow dividends over time. It holds a limited number of stocks spread across financials, tech, industrials and health care, with Broadcom and TSMC the largest at about 4% each.
CGDV: An actively managed fund from Capital Group of large US companies that pay dividends, picked by the firm's research analysts rather than an index. It leans toward big tech, with Microsoft, NVIDIA and Broadcom about 17% of it.
CGGO: An actively managed global stock fund from Capital Group, holding companies around the world its managers think can grow. Chip makers loom large: Taiwan Semiconductor, Micron and SK Hynix are about 18% of it.
CGGR: US stocks that Capital Group's managers think offer strong growth potential, with a small slice allowed outside the US. It is actively managed rather than tracking an index, and Meta, Tesla, Broadcom and NVIDIA are its biggest holdings at about 24% together.
CGMM: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, picked by Capital Group's managers. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings, such as Bloom Energy and Exelon, only about 2% each.
CGMS: An actively managed US bond fund mixing different kinds of income-paying debt, such as company bonds, mortgage-related bonds and higher-yield bonds, to aim for a high level of income. It is widely spread, with no single holding above about 3%.
CGMU: Municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, chosen by Capital Group managers, with interest mostly exempt from regular federal income tax. Most are medium maturity, and the holdings are very spread out, with the biggest only around 1%.
CGUS: An actively managed US stock fund from Capital Group, holding companies its managers expect to grow in value or pay dividends. NVIDIA, Broadcom, Microsoft and Amazon are about 24% of it.
CGXU: A manager-picked fund of growth-oriented companies based outside the US, including emerging markets. It holds a limited number of stocks, and Taiwan Semiconductor, SoftBank and First Quantum Minerals are among its largest, with tech the biggest sector at about 26%.
CIBR: Companies that make cybersecurity software and hardware, such as firewalls, threat detection and network protection, tracked by the Nasdaq CTA Cybersecurity index. Concentrated: Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, CrowdStrike and Cisco make up about 35% of it.
CMF: Bonds issued by California cities, schools and agencies, tracked by an index of investment grade California municipal bonds. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and holdings are very spread out, with no single bond above about 1% of the fund.
COPX: Global companies that mine copper, tracked by a Global X index. It is a bet on one industry, nearly all materials, with BHP, Teck, Hudbay, Southern Copper and First Quantum each at about 5%.
CORO: An actively managed fund that holds other iShares country funds, shifting money toward countries outside the US that its managers favor. Japan is about 20% and Canada about 13%, so a few countries drive the result at any time.
COWZ: About 100 large and mid-sized US companies that generate the most free cash flow (cash left over after expenses and investments) relative to their value. It is rules-based and spread fairly evenly, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward energy, health care and industrials.
CWB: Convertible bonds, which are company bonds that can be swapped for shares of the issuer's stock, tracking a Bloomberg convertibles index. They combine some bond-like income with stock-like swings, and they are spread across many companies, mostly in technology.
DBEF: Stocks of large companies in developed markets outside North America (Europe, Japan, Australia), tracked by an MSCI EAFE index, but with currency hedging. The hedge offsets moves between those currencies and the US dollar, so mostly the stock prices matter to you.
DBMF: A managed futures fund that tries to copy how trend-following hedge funds trade, using futures contracts on currencies, bonds, stock indexes and commodities. It goes long or short as trends change, so it can behave differently from stocks and bonds, and much of it sits in cash and short-term bonds.
DCOR: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, run by Dimensional, which tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market index would. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are still about 16% of it.
DEM: Large emerging market companies that pay high dividends, weighted by how much cash they pay out rather than by size. Holdings are spread over Taiwan, China, Brazil, South Africa and others, and tilt toward chipmakers and big banks like MediaTek and China Construction Bank.
DFAC: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, run by Dimensional, which tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market index would. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are still about 15% of it.
DFAE: A broad mix of emerging market stocks (such as Taiwan, China, India and Korea), chosen by Dimensional using its own size and value rules rather than a single index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13% of it, and technology is around 40%.
DFAI: Thousands of stocks from developed countries outside the US, of all sizes, with extra weight on smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than a plain market index would hold. It is spread very thin: the biggest holding, ASML, is only about 1.6% of the fund, and financials lead.
DFAR: US real estate companies, mostly REITs that own property such as apartments, warehouses, data centers and shopping centers, weighted by size. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are about 20% of it, and REITs usually pay out a lot of income.
DFAS: Small US companies of all styles, bought in proportion to their market value using Dimensional's rules. It holds well over a thousand stocks, so no single holding is more than about 0.3% of the fund.
DFAT: A broad group of US small and mid-sized companies that look cheap compared with their size and are also more profitable, picked by Dimensional's rules rather than an index. It is spread across hundreds of stocks, with financials the largest sector at about 29%.
DFAU: A broad mix of US stocks of all sizes, tilted by Dimensional toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than the overall market. The biggest names are still NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, which together are about 18% of it.
DFAX: Stocks of companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US, run by Dimensional with a tilt toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms. It is very spread out, and Taiwan Semiconductor, the largest holding, is only about 3% across its two listings.
DFCF: A broad US investment grade bond fund from Dimensional, mixing government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that mostly mature within about 20 years. It is actively managed rather than tracking a standard index, and several of its largest positions are mortgage bonds.
DFEM: A broad mix of emerging market stocks (such as Taiwan, China, India and Korea), chosen by Dimensional using its own size and value rules rather than a single index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 10% of it, and technology is around 40%.
DFGP: Government and company bonds from the US and abroad, mostly investment grade, including US mortgage bonds and Japanese government bonds. Dimensional runs it with a rules-based but flexible approach, and it aims to hedge foreign currency back to US dollars.
DFGR: Real estate companies from around the world, including emerging markets, weighted by company size. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix, which own health care properties, warehouses and data centers, are about 20% of the fund.
DFGV: US government and agency bonds that mature in about five to fifteen years, chosen by Dimensional's rules for low risk. It sticks to high quality government debt, so it is a middle-length bond fund with little credit risk and no stock exposure.
DFIC: A broad mix of stocks from developed countries outside the US, covering companies of all sizes and leaning toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones. Thousands of holdings keep it spread out: the top few, such as ASML and Shell, are only about 1% each.
DFIS: Thousands of small companies in developed countries outside the US, bought in roughly market-size proportions, with a lean toward cheaper and more profitable ones. It is extremely spread out, with every holding under 1%, and industrials, materials and consumer firms are the largest groups.
DFIV: Large companies from developed countries outside the US that look cheap relative to their book value, picked by Dimensional's rules-based approach. It also tries to limit taxable gains by timing its trades, and Shell, TotalEnergies and Santander are among its larger holdings.
DFLV: Large US companies that Dimensional considers cheap relative to their size, with extra weight on the cheapest and most profitable. JPMorgan, Amazon and Exxon Mobil are among the biggest holdings, and it leans toward financials, health care, energy and industrials.
DFMC: A broad basket of very small US companies (micro caps), bought in proportion to their size by Dimensional Fund Advisors. It holds a great many tiny stocks, none above about 0.5%, so no single company moves it much.
DFSD: A mix of investment-grade bonds, mostly government and corporate, that mature within about five years, chosen by Dimensional's managers. Because the bonds are short term, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than a regular bond fund, and the holdings are very spread out.
DFSV: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their book value, picked by Dimensional's rules-based but actively run approach. It holds hundreds of stocks, with no single one above about 1%, and leans toward financials, industrials and energy.
DFUS: The whole US stock market, buying companies of all sizes in proportion to their market value. It works like a broad index fund, so it is top-heavy toward big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of the fund.
DFUV: US companies of all sizes that Dimensional considers value stocks, meaning priced low relative to measures like their book value. It holds a wide range, led by JPMorgan, Amazon, Exxon and Johnson & Johnson, each between roughly 3% and 5%.
DGRO: US companies with a record of growing their dividends that are expected to keep paying them, following a Morningstar index. Holdings are weighted by dividends paid, so it is spread out: the top names, such as Microsoft and JPMorgan, are each about 3%.
DGRW: US companies that pay dividends and have strong profitability and growing earnings, weighted by the dividends they pay rather than by size. It still leans on big tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple together are about 17% of the fund.
DIA: The 30 big US companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, weighted by share price rather than company size. That odd weighting means the higher-priced stocks count more: Goldman Sachs, Caterpillar and Microsoft are about 26% of the fund.
DIHP: Large companies outside the US that Dimensional rates as highly profitable, bought in a size-aware way. Roche, ASML and Nestle are the biggest names, and holdings are spread over industrials, technology, health care and financials.
DISV: Small, cheaper-looking companies in developed countries outside the US, picked by Dimensional using value measures such as low prices relative to book value. It holds thousands of names, with no holding above about 1%, spread across industrials, materials, financials and consumer firms.
DIVO: A fund of dividend-paying US companies picked by a manager, which also sells covered call options on some of them to bring in extra income. The options give up some of the gains in strong markets; Caterpillar, Apple and Microsoft are each about 5 to 7% of it.
DLCU: The 500 large US companies of the S&P 500, held in about the same proportions as the index, managed by Dimensional. It is top-heavy with tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of the fund.
DLN: About 300 of the largest US dividend-paying companies, with each one weighted by the total dividends it pays rather than by its size. That tilts it toward steady payers like banks, health care and consumer staples, and it is far less top-heavy than most large-company funds.
DON: US mid-sized companies that pay dividends, with each stock weighted by the dividends it pays rather than by its size. It is spread thin, with the largest holding only about 1% of the fund.
DRAM: Companies that make memory chips and related storage products, such as Samsung, SK hynix and Seagate, sometimes held through swaps (contracts that mimic owning the stock). It is a narrow theme fund, with Samsung and SK hynix making up roughly a third of it.
DSI: About 400 large US companies chosen for strong environmental, social and governance records, tracking the MSCI KLD 400 Social Index. It is tech-heavy and top-heavy: NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 23% of it, and technology is around 45% of the fund.
DUHP: Large US companies chosen by Dimensional because they are unusually profitable compared with their peers. NVIDIA, Apple, Eli Lilly and Microsoft are about 24% of it, so it still leans toward big names.
DVY: About 100 US stocks with some of the highest dividend yields (annual dividend relative to share price), subject to rules on dividend history and payout. It leans toward financials, utilities and consumer companies, and holds more mid-sized firms than the big tech names.
DXJ: Large Japanese companies, mainly exporters, with a currency hedge added that protects against a falling yen versus the US dollar. Banks like Mitsubishi UFJ and Sumitomo Mitsui, plus Toyota, are among its biggest holdings, and it leans toward industrials and financials.
DXUV: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes that leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones than the overall market, following Dimensional's research-based rules. Despite that tilt, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Apple are still around 14% of it.
DYNF: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US stocks that shifts its mix of investing styles, such as value, quality or momentum, based on a model's view of the market. It currently looks like the big tech heavy market, with NVIDIA and Apple about 15%.
EAGG: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage bonds, like a standard aggregate bond index but screened for environmental, social and governance factors. It is spread across thousands of bonds, none above about 0.5%.
EAGL: An actively managed fund where Eagle Capital picks a small group of companies, US and foreign, that it thinks are good businesses at fair prices. It is concentrated: Amazon, MercadoLibre, UnitedHealth and Taiwan Semiconductor are each about 7%.
EDV: US Treasury STRIPS that mature in 20 to 30 years. These are zero-coupon bonds that pay nothing until the end, which makes their price swing a lot when interest rates change, much more than a normal Treasury fund.
EEM: Large and mid-sized stocks from emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India, South Korea and Brazil, following an MSCI index. It is concentrated in a few giants: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 22% of it.
EEMV: Emerging market stocks chosen and weighted to swing less in price than the broader emerging market index, following an MSCI index. It is spread out, with the largest holding, SK Hynix, only about 3%.
EFA: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, such as Japan, the UK and France, tracking the MSCI EAFE index. It excludes the US and Canada, and financials and industrials are the biggest sectors.
EFAV: Stocks from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and Asia (excluding the US and Canada) picked to have lower price swings than the broader market, using the MSCI EAFE Minimum Volatility Index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
EFG: Growth-oriented large and mid-sized companies from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and the Far East (not the US or Canada), tracking the MSCI EAFE Growth index. ASML is the biggest holding at about 6%, and industrials and technology lead.
EFV: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US and Canada that look cheap on measures like price relative to earnings or book value. It leans heavily toward financials, about 40% of the fund, with banks like HSBC among the top holdings.
EMB: US dollar bonds issued by governments and government-linked companies in emerging markets, tracking a J.P. Morgan index. It pays more interest than US Treasuries because these borrowers are riskier, and Argentina and Ecuador appear among its larger holdings.
EMLC: Bonds issued by emerging-market governments, such as Brazil, South Africa and Mexico, paid in each country's own currency rather than US dollars. Returns depend on both the bonds and how those currencies move against the dollar; it tracks a J.P. Morgan index.
EMLP: Mostly pipeline and other energy infrastructure companies in the US and Canada, picked by a manager rather than an index. Many are partnerships that pay out lots of income, and Enterprise Products and Energy Transfer are about 16% of it.
EMXC: Stocks from emerging markets such as Taiwan, India and South Korea, but leaving out China, tracking the MSCI Emerging Markets ex China index. It is chip-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix together are about 36% of the fund.
ESGD: Stocks from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and Asia outside North America, based on the MSCI EAFE index but tilted toward companies with better environmental, social and governance scores. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest at about 3%.
ESGE: Stocks from emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, tilted toward companies with better environmental and social scores. It is top-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 15%, and with Samsung the two are around 23%.
ESGU: Large US companies chosen from the MSCI USA index, tilted toward firms with better environmental, social and governance scores while staying close to the index's overall makeup. Tech dominates: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet together are roughly 24% of the fund.
ESGV: US stocks screened to leave out companies in areas like weapons, fossil fuels and tobacco or with poor ESG records, then weighted by size like a broad market fund. Tech heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon are around 26% of it.
ETHA: A fund that holds actual ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, so you can own it through a regular brokerage account instead of a crypto exchange. Its price moves with ether, which can swing sharply, and it holds no stocks or bonds.
EUFN: Banks, insurers and other financial companies from developed European countries, following an MSCI index. HSBC alone is about 10% of it, and Santander, Allianz and UBS add roughly another 15%.
EVTR: An actively managed bond fund holding a mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with the manager free to look beyond the standard bond index. Treasuries and mortgage bonds make up a big share of its largest holdings.
EWC: A broad group of large and mid-size Canadian companies, tracked by the MSCI Canada index. It is dominated by banks, with Royal Bank of Canada and Toronto Dominion about 15% together, and financials, energy and materials make up around 70%.
EWJ: Large and mid-sized Japanese companies, tracking the MSCI Japan index. It is well spread, with Mitsubishi UFJ, Toyota, SoftBank and Tokyo Electron the biggest names but each only about 3% to 4% of the fund, and it is priced in US dollars with the yen exposure unhedged.
EWT: Taiwanese companies, tracking the MSCI Taiwan index. It is heavy in chip makers and electronics: Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 19%, and with MediaTek, Delta Electronics and Hon Hai the top four are about 37%.
EWU: Large and mid-sized companies based in the United Kingdom, following an MSCI index. It leans on a few big names: HSBC, AstraZeneca and Shell are about 27% of the fund.
EWY: South Korean stocks, tracking the MSCI South Korea index of the country's large and mid-sized companies. It is heavily concentrated in chipmakers: SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics together are about 55% of the fund.
EWZ: Large Brazilian companies, tracked by an MSCI Brazil index. It is concentrated: Vale, Nu Holdings, Itau and Petrobras are about 35% of it, and banks, oil and mining dominate, so it moves with Brazil's economy and currency.
EZU: Large and mid-sized companies from the countries that use the euro, such as Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands, tracked by an MSCI index. It holds no UK or Swiss stocks, and ASML, the chip equipment maker, is about 8% of it.
FBCG: A manager-picked fund of large, well-established US companies that are expected to grow faster than average. It is heavily tilted to tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about a third of the fund, and technology is more than half.
FBND: A broad mix of US bonds, including Treasuries, corporate and mortgage bonds, with Fidelity's managers using the Bloomberg U.S. Universal Bond Index as a guide. It is actively managed, so it can differ from the index, and US Treasuries make up its biggest individual holdings.
FBTC: A fund that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its price, so owning shares is a way to get bitcoin exposure through a regular brokerage account. It holds no stocks or bonds, and its value swings with the price of bitcoin.
FDL: The 100 highest-yielding US stocks with a record of steady dividends, according to Morningstar, so it is built for income. It is concentrated in a few names, with Chevron, Verizon and Philip Morris making up about 20%, and leans toward consumer staples, utilities and energy.
FDN: US internet companies, tracking the Dow Jones Internet Composite Index, which covers e-commerce, social media, search and internet software and hardware firms. Amazon and Meta are about 20% of it, and the top ten names are around half of the fund.
FDVV: Large and mid-sized US companies that pay above-average dividends, picked by a Fidelity index. Unlike many dividend funds it holds a lot of big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, with banks and consumer companies behind them.
FELC: A fund that mostly holds S&P 500 stocks but lets Fidelity tilt toward ones its research favors, aiming to beat the index a little. It is similar to the S&P 500, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 19% of it.
FELG: Large US growth companies from the Russell 1000 Growth Index, with the manager tilting holdings up or down to try to beat that index. It is very concentrated in tech: NVIDIA is over 13%, and NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about 27% of the fund.
FENI: Stocks from developed markets outside North America, built around the MSCI EAFE index but with Fidelity adjusting the mix to try to beat it. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest holding at about 4%.
FESM: Small US companies similar to the Russell 2000, but chosen by a Fidelity research-driven approach rather than simply buying the whole index. It holds many small stocks, each about 1% or less, with health care, technology, financials and industrials leading.
FEZ: The 50 biggest companies across the euro currency countries, tracking the EURO STOXX 50 index. It is concentrated: ASML, a Dutch chip equipment maker, is about 10% of the fund, and banks and industrial companies fill much of the rest.
FHLC: US health care companies, from drug makers to insurers and device makers, following an MSCI index of the sector. Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie are about 29% of it.
FIMU: Municipal bonds of medium length, issued by states, cities and public agencies, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is spread across many bonds, with none above about 1%, and several of the largest come from public gas and energy authorities.
FLJP: Japanese companies of all sizes, tracked by a FTSE index that caps how much any one firm can weigh. It is broadly spread out across banks, electronics and carmakers, and the biggest holdings, like Mitsubishi UFJ, Tokyo Electron and Toyota, are each about 3%.
FLOT: Investment grade bonds whose interest payments reset regularly with short-term rates, so the price stays fairly steady. It tracks a Bloomberg index of these floating rate notes from companies, banks and groups like the World Bank.
FLTR: Investment-grade floating rate notes, bonds whose interest rate resets as short-term rates move, mostly issued by banks. That keeps price swings small when rates change, and no single issuer is above about 1%.
FLTW: Taiwanese companies of all sizes, tracked by a FTSE index that caps how much any one company can weigh. It is concentrated in electronics: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 20% of the fund and the top four holdings are around 40%.
FLXR: An actively managed bond fund from TCW that moves flexibly across credit, currencies and interest rates around the world. The manager decides where to invest, so it does not follow a standard bond index.
FMDE: A fund that mainly holds Russell Midcap stocks, but lets Fidelity tilt toward ones its research favors, aiming to beat the index a little. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%.
FNDA: Small US companies, picked and weighted by business size such as sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. It holds about a thousand names with none above 1%, so it is very evenly spread.
FNDE: Large emerging market companies (such as Taiwan, China, Brazil and India) chosen and weighted by business size measures like sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 6% of it, and financials, technology and energy are the biggest areas.
FNDF: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, chosen and weighted by sales, cash flow and dividends rather than market value. Samsung, Shell and TotalEnergies are among its top holdings, and it tilts toward value-style stocks like banks and energy firms.
FNDX: Large US companies picked and weighted by business size measures like sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. That makes it less tilted toward the biggest stocks than a regular index fund, though Apple, Intel, Alphabet and Microsoft are still its largest holdings.
FPE: Preferred stocks and other income-paying bonds, mostly from big banks, insurers and utilities, which pay a fixed dividend and rank ahead of regular shares. It is actively managed and built for income rather than growth, and it is roughly half preferred stocks and half bonds.
FRDM: Emerging market stocks, with countries weighted by how free they score on personal and economic freedom measures. Chip makers lead: Samsung, SK hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor are about a third of the fund.
FREI: An actively managed mix of real estate related investments: mostly bonds and loans, with some real estate company stocks and preferred shares. It is built for income, and well known property owners like American Tower, Welltower and Prologis show up as small holdings.
FSEC: Mortgage-backed and other securitized bonds, which bundle many loans together and pass on the payments, mostly backed by US government agencies. It is actively managed, and it is built for steady income with investment grade quality.
FTCS: Large US companies chosen for strong finances, such as lots of cash and high returns on their capital, from a Nasdaq index of big US stocks. It holds about 50 names in similar-sized stakes of around 2%, spread over financials, industrials, consumer staples and health care.
FTEC: US technology companies, from software to chips to hardware, tracking the MSCI USA IMI Information Technology 25/50 index. It is very top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 44% of the fund.
FTSM: Short-term US dollar bonds, mostly government and investment-grade corporate, run actively to keep average maturity under three years. Because of that the price barely moves, and income tracks short-term interest rates, with holdings spread very widely.
FV: A fund that holds five First Trust sector funds, picked by a rules-based ranking of which sectors have recently done best. Each gets about 20%, so the mix changes as the rankings do.
FVD: About 200 US dividend payers that Value Line rates as safe and financially sound, weighted roughly equally. Because each stock is only a sliver (around 0.4%), no company dominates, and it leans toward financials, utilities and industrials.
FWD: An actively managed global stock fund that looks for companies likely to benefit from big technology and industry shifts. It is spread out, with Broadcom, AMD, Samsung and NVIDIA each only about 2% to 3%.
FXI: About 50 of the biggest Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong, tracked by an index of large caps. It is fairly concentrated: Alibaba, Tencent and two huge state banks make up about a third of the fund.
GBIL: US Treasury bills and notes maturing in one year or less, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bonds are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
GBTC: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and aims to follow its price, so its shares rise and fall with bitcoin. It holds no stocks or bonds, and bitcoin prices can swing widely.
GCOW: Large companies from around the world that pay high dividends and also produce lots of free cash flow, meaning cash left after running the business. It is spread out, with the largest holdings only about 2% each.
GDX: Companies that mine gold and a few that mine silver, held in proportion to their size, tracking the NYSE Arca Gold Miners index. It is concentrated, with Agnico Eagle, Newmont and Barrick making up about 29%, and it swings with gold prices.
GDXJ: Smaller gold and silver mining companies from around the world, tracked by a VanEck index. Miners tend to swing more than gold itself, and it is spread across many names, with Evolution, Equinox and Alamos each about 6%.
GGOV: An actively managed fund of government bonds from countries around the world, with the currency exposure hedged back to US dollars. The hedging removes most of the swings from foreign currencies, so results depend mainly on interest rates in those countries.
GLD: A fund that holds physical gold bars in vaults, so its price follows the price of gold. It owns no companies and pays no income, so what it is worth depends only on gold.
GLDM: Physical gold bars held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of gold. It holds no companies and pays no income, so any gain or loss comes only from the price of gold.
GNR: Large global companies tied to natural resources: energy, mining, agriculture and timber, tracking an S&P index of 90 of them. Materials are about half and energy about a third, with BHP, Nutrien, ExxonMobil and Shell among the largest holdings.
GOVT: A broad mix of US Treasury bonds of all lengths, from short to very long, weighted by size. Backed by the government, it gives a middle level of interest rate sensitivity, since the short and long bonds balance out.
GPIQ: Holds the Nasdaq-100's large, tech-heavy stocks and sells call options on them to earn extra income, which pays a premium but caps gains in strong rallies. Technology is about 60% of it, with NVIDIA and Apple among the biggest holdings.
GPIX: Holds the S&P 500's large US companies and sells call options on them to collect extra income, which brings in a premium but caps gains when stocks surge. NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are the largest holdings, and technology is about 40% of it.
GRID: Companies that build and equip the electric grid, such as makers of grid equipment, smart meters and power infrastructure, tracking a Nasdaq Clean Edge index. Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB and Quanta are each about 8%, around a third together.
GRNY: An actively managed fund of about 35 large US stocks picked by Fundstrat using a mix of research and what it sees as major market themes. Each holding is a small slice, around 2% to 3%, so it is more evenly spread than most big stock funds.
GSIE: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked to tilt toward four traits: low risk, value, quality and momentum. It is very spread out, with the biggest holding, chip equipment maker ASML, only about 2% of the fund, and financials are around 29%.
GSLC: Large US companies in roughly the same mix as the broad market, but with a rules-based tilt toward stocks showing good value, momentum, quality and low volatility. Tech giants still dominate: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of the fund.
GUNR: Global companies that produce natural resources, such as miners, oil and gas producers, fertilizer and farming firms, and timber. About half is in materials and a third in energy, with Exxon Mobil, Corteva and BHP among the biggest holdings.
GVI: A mix of US Treasuries, other government-backed bonds and bonds from solid companies, with medium-term maturities, following a Bloomberg index. It holds thousands of bonds, so no single one is more than about 1%.
HDV: About 75 US companies with high dividend yields and strong financial health, from the Morningstar Dividend Yield Focus index. It is concentrated in a few sectors: consumer staples and energy are over half, and Exxon, AbbVie and Chevron are each around 6% to 8%.
HEFA: Developed-market stocks outside the US and Canada (Europe, Japan, Australia and more) held through the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, with currency hedges added. The hedges reduce the effect of the US dollar moving against the euro, yen and pound on what you earn.
HELO: A large US stock fund that also uses options to cushion the fund against big market drops. The options are rolled forward in stages, which limits some of the upside too, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 20% of the stocks.
HGER: Gets exposure to a broad mix of commodity futures (things like energy, metals and farm goods) through a quantitative index, using swaps held in an overseas subsidiary. Most of the money actually sits in Treasuries and similar safe assets as backing, so the commodity swaps drive the results.
HYD: Tax-exempt bonds from US states, cities and agencies with weaker credit ratings, so they pay higher interest but carry more risk of default. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%, including some Puerto Rico and tobacco settlement bonds.
HYG: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest to make up for the greater risk of default. It holds hundreds of bonds, each under 1%, so no single company matters much.
HYMB: Tax-exempt bonds from US states, cities and agencies with weaker credit ratings, following an ICE index. They pay higher interest but carry more risk, and Puerto Rico bonds are among the biggest holdings at a few percent each.
IAGG: Investment grade bonds from governments and companies outside the US, with currency swings hedged back into US dollars. China government bonds are among its larger holdings, and the hedging removes most of the effect of exchange rates.
IALT: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, bonds and alternative strategies, aiming to hold up in both strong and stressful markets. It works more like a multi-strategy blend than a regular stock or bond fund.
IAU: A trust that holds physical gold bars, so its price follows the price of gold bullion. It is not actively managed, owns no companies and pays no income, so what it is worth depends only on gold.
IAUM: A fund backed by physical gold held in a vault, so its price follows the gold price. It has a small share price, so it is easy to buy a little, and it pays no income and holds no stocks.
IBB: US-listed biotech companies, which develop new drugs and therapies, tracking a biotechnology index. Vertex, Amgen and Gilead are about 23% of it, and it is non-diversified, meaning it can hold larger stakes in fewer companies.
IBDS: A basket of bonds from financially solid US companies that all mature in 2027, after which the fund shuts down around December 2027 and hands back what is left. It owns hundreds of bonds, and no single company is more than about 1%.
IBDT: A basket of US investment grade company bonds that all mature in 2028. As the bonds mature the fund winds down and closes in December 2028, so it behaves a bit like a single bond, with holdings spread across hundreds of issuers like CVS and Pfizer.
IBDU: A basket of bonds from financially solid US companies that all mature in 2029, after which the fund shuts down around December 2029 and hands back what is left. It owns hundreds of bonds, and no single company is more than about 1%.
IBIT: A trust that holds actual bitcoin, so its price tracks the price of bitcoin without needing a crypto exchange account. It owns no companies and pays no income, and as a single asset it can swing sharply.
ICVT: Convertible bonds, which are bonds from companies that can be swapped for the company's stock, tracked by a Bloomberg index. They sit between bonds and stocks, so they tend to move with the stock market, and no single bond is above about 3%.
IDEF: An actively managed fund of defense and related industrial companies, plus technology firms, from the US and abroad, picked by a manager. RTX, Palantir, Lockheed Martin and Rolls-Royce are about 19% of it.
IDEV: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Japan, the UK, Canada and Europe, following an MSCI index. It is spread out, with the top holding, ASML, about 2%, and financials the largest sector.
IDMO: Large companies in developed markets outside the US that have recently been rising faster than others, picked and weighted by an S&P momentum index. At the moment it leans heavily toward European and Canadian banks like HSBC, Santander and Toronto Dominion.
IDV: About 100 high dividend paying companies in developed markets outside North America, picked by a Dow Jones index. It leans toward banks, energy and utilities, with TotalEnergies, British American Tobacco and Enel among the biggest holdings.
IEF: US Treasury bonds that mature in seven to ten years, following an index of such bonds. Backed by the government, with a price that reacts to interest rates more than short-term Treasuries do but less than 20 year bonds.
IEFA: Tracks an MSCI index of large, mid-sized and small companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, mainly Europe, Japan and Australia. Financials and industrials are the biggest sectors, and ASML, HSBC and Roche are top holdings, each a small slice.
IEI: US Treasury bonds that have between three and seven years left until they mature, so it sits in the middle of the Treasury range. Government-backed with no credit risk to speak of, but its price still moves with interest rates.
IEMG: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India, Taiwan and South Korea, following an MSCI index of large, mid-sized and small companies. It is top-heavy in Asian chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 25% together.
IEUR: A broad mix of large, mid and small European companies from the UK, Switzerland, France, Germany and others, tracked by an MSCI index. It is well spread: ASML is the biggest holding at about 4%, and financials are about a quarter of it.
IFRA: US companies tied to building and running infrastructure, such as utilities, railroads, construction and materials firms. The stakes are fairly even: the largest holdings, Caterpillar, NextEra and Union Pacific, are each only about 4%.
IGF: Large infrastructure companies around the world, such as airports, toll roads, electric and gas utilities and pipelines. It is split roughly evenly between utilities and industrials, with some energy, and holds Spanish, Australian, US and Canadian names.
IGIB: US dollar bonds from financially sound companies, with five to ten years left until they mature. They pay more interest than Treasuries, move more with rates than short-term bond funds, and are spread across hundreds of issuers with none above about 0.2%.
IGM: A wider take on tech that holds technology companies plus some related ones, such as internet and media firms. NVIDIA, Apple, Broadcom and Microsoft are each about 8%, so around 31% of the fund sits in those four.
IGSB: US dollar bonds from financially sound companies, but only those maturing in one to five years. Shorter maturities mean its price moves less than longer corporate bond funds when interest rates change, and it spreads across a very large number of issuers.
IGV: US software companies, from enterprise software to security, tracked by an S&P software index. It is concentrated: Palo Alto Networks, Microsoft, Palantir and CrowdStrike together are about a third of it, and it is almost all technology.
IHI: US companies that make medical devices, such as heart valves, surgical robots and joint implants, following a Dow Jones index. Abbott, Intuitive Surgical and Stryker are about 44% of the fund.
IJH: About 400 mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 index, weighted by size. No single holding is much above 1%, and industrials, technology and financials are the biggest sectors.
IJJ: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that look cheaper compared with their earnings and sales. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 1.5%, and leans toward financials, industrials and consumer companies.
IJK: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that show faster growth, tracked by an index. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward industrials, technology and health care rather than the mega-cap tech giants.
IJR: About 600 small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 index, which also screens for profitability. No holding tops about 1%, so it is very spread out across financials, technology and industrials.
IJS: Smaller US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that look cheap relative to their size and fundamentals, a style known as value. It holds hundreds of stocks with no single one above about 1.3%, leaning toward financials, consumer discretionary and technology.
IJT: Smaller US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that show the strongest growth traits, such as rising sales and earnings. It is very spread out: the biggest holdings are only about 1% each, across technology, industrials, health care and financials.
ILF: About 40 of the largest companies in Latin America, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, following an S&P index. It is top-heavy in miners and banks: Vale, Nu Holdings and Itau are about a quarter of the fund.
IMCG: Medium sized US companies that Morningstar's index rates as having above-average growth, like Fortinet, Snowflake and Freeport-McMoRan. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is above about 1.5%, so it is spread out, with tilts toward tech and industrials.
IMTM: Large and mid size companies in developed markets outside the US that have recently been going up faster than their peers, tracked through an MSCI momentum index. The mix changes as winners change, and it currently includes ASML, HSBC, Royal Bank of Canada and Roche.
INDA: Large and mid-sized Indian companies, tracking the MSCI India Index. Banks are the biggest group at about 30% of the fund, and Reliance Industries and HDFC Bank are each over 6%, so a few big names matter.
INTF: Stocks from large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted toward traits like value, quality and momentum. It stays broad, with ASML the largest holding at only about 2%.
IOO: About 100 of the world's largest companies, mostly American, from an S&P index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 30% of it, and technology is roughly half.
IQLT: Large and mid-sized companies from developed markets outside the US, picked for high quality: strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, from the MSCI World ex USA Quality index. ASML is the largest holding at around 5%, and financials and industrials lead.
IQMM: A money market fund that holds only very short-term US government debt and similar safe cash-like holdings. It is built to keep a stable price while paying interest that follows short-term rates, and it is designed to fit rules for backing payment stablecoins.
ISTB: US government, corporate and mortgage bonds that mature in one to five years, tracking a short-term investment-grade bond index. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, its price should move less than a fund of longer bonds, and no single bond is above about 1%.
ITA: US aerospace and defense companies, tracking a Dow Jones index of the sector, including makers of jet engines, aircraft and weapons. It is concentrated: General Electric, RTX and Boeing together are about 46% of the fund.
ITOT: Almost the entire US stock market, from large to small companies, tracking the S&P Total Market Index. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 16% of it, and technology is about 38%.
IUSB: A wide mix of US dollar bonds in one fund: Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds, company bonds and some higher-yield and foreign-issued debt, following a Bloomberg index. It is a one-fund take on the whole bond market, with thousands of holdings and no big single position.
IUSG: Large and mid-sized US companies with growth traits from the S&P 900, weighted by size. It is tilted toward tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 26% of it, and technology makes up over half the fund.
IUSV: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, tracking the S&P 900 Value index. Value funds lean toward financials, health care and energy, and Apple is the largest holding at about 7%.
IVE: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, large US companies that score as value stocks on measures like price relative to earnings and book value. Despite the value label, Apple is about 7% of it and technology is the largest sector.
IVLU: Large and mid size companies in developed markets outside the US, picked because they look cheap compared to their earnings and book value, based on an MSCI index. It leans toward banks, carmakers and other cyclical firms, with HSBC, BNP Paribas and Toyota among the top holdings.
IVOO: About 400 mid-sized US companies, tracking the S&P MidCap 400 Index, which sits between big blue chips and small caps. It is widely spread, with the biggest holdings under 2% each, and industrials, technology and financials are the largest groups.
IVV: iShares' version of the S&P 500: roughly 500 large US companies, weighted by size. It holds essentially the same stocks as other S&P 500 funds, so about 40% is technology and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are around 18%.
IVW: The growth half of the S&P 500: large US companies with faster growth traits, weighted by size. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple around 27% together and technology more than half.
IWB: The roughly 1,000 largest US companies, held in proportion to their size, following the Russell 1000 index. It covers most of the US stock market by value, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 17% of it, with technology around 39%.
IWD: Large and mid-sized US value stocks from the Russell 1000 Value index, meaning companies that look cheaply priced. Amazon and Apple are the top holdings at around 6% each, and financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
IWF: Large and mid-sized US growth stocks from the Russell 1000 Growth index, weighted by size. It is heavy in tech at roughly 57%, and NVIDIA alone is nearly 14% of the fund.
IWM: Nearly 2,000 of the smallest companies in the Russell 3000, making it one of the best known small-company US funds. Each holding is a tiny slice, around 0.4% at most, spread over health care, financials, technology and industrials.
IWN: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, a value subset of the Russell 2000 index. Financials are the biggest sector at about 28%, and with hundreds of stocks no single one is above about 1%.
IWO: Small US companies with faster expected growth, a subset of the Russell 2000 index. Health care is the biggest sector at about 30%, followed by technology, and no single stock is more than about 1% of the fund.
IWP: US mid-sized companies expected to grow faster than average, tracking the Russell Midcap Growth index. It leans toward software and tech firms, and the biggest holdings such as Datadog, Snowflake and Cloudflare are only about 2% each.
IWR: Mid-sized US companies, the smaller roughly 800 of the Russell 1000 index, weighted by company size. No single stock matters much here: the biggest holdings are each only about 0.6%, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
IWS: Mid-sized US companies that look cheap relative to their size, tracking the Russell Midcap Value index. It holds hundreds of stocks with no position above about 1%, spread across financials, industrials, technology, energy and real estate.
IWV: Nearly the whole US stock market, about 3,000 companies of all sizes, tracking the Russell 3000 index. It is dominated by big companies: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon make up about 19% of the fund.
IWX: Large US companies from the Russell Top 200 that look cheaper than the rest, with lower prices relative to their book value and slower expected growth. Even so, Amazon, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
IWY: The growth-oriented half of the 200 largest US companies, tracking the Russell Top 200 Growth index. Very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Broadcom are about a third of it, and tech makes up well over half.
IXJ: About 100 of the largest health care companies around the world, like drugmakers, device makers and insurers, tracking an S&P index. It is top heavy: Eli Lilly is about 11% of the fund, and most holdings are US companies.
IXN: Large technology companies from around the world, following an S&P index that caps the biggest names so they cannot dominate. It is still top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 32% of the fund, with Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom next.
IXUS: Thousands of stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, weighted by company size, following an MSCI index of non-US markets. It is spread widely: the largest holding, Taiwan Semiconductor, is only about 4% of it, and financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
IYF: US financial companies: banks, insurers, asset managers and payment firms, following a Dow Jones index of the sector. Two names dominate: Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan are each about 11% of the fund.
IYH: US health care companies, such as drugmakers, insurers and medical device makers, tracked by an index. It is top heavy: Eli Lilly is about 15% of the fund, and Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie together are about a third.
IYR: US real estate companies, mostly real estate investment trusts that own buildings and pass on rental income, tracked by a Dow Jones index. It is top heavy: Welltower and Prologis are about 20% of the fund.
IYW: US technology companies, covering software, hardware, semiconductors and internet firms, in proportion to their size. It is very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft alone make up about 38% of the fund.
JAAA: An actively managed fund of AAA rated collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds, with the safest slices held. Their payments float with short-term interest rates, so it can pay more income than plain short-term bonds.
JAVA: A manager-picked fund of US large companies that look attractively priced relative to their long-term growth potential. It differs from a plain value index fund because the manager chooses the stocks, and Amazon, Microsoft and Apple are among the biggest holdings.
JBND: An actively managed bond fund from JPMorgan that aims to beat the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It holds a mix of US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with managers picking them instead of copying an index.
JCPB: An actively managed fund that mainly holds US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds, plus a smaller slice of riskier debt. Managers choose the holdings rather than following an index, and the average maturity usually runs five to twenty years.
JEPI: An actively managed fund of large US stocks, picked for lower risk, that also sells call options on the S&P 500 to generate extra income, and those options limit how much it gains in strong markets. Holdings are spread out, none above about 2%.
JEPQ: An actively managed fund of Nasdaq-100 style stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income, and the options cap how much it gains in strong rallies. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Micron about 18% of it.
JGLO: An actively managed portfolio of large companies from developed markets around the world, picked by the manager rather than by an index. It is heavy in US tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 18% of it, and technology is around a third of the fund.
JGRO: An actively managed fund where JPMorgan picks large US growth companies by hand, rather than following an index. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Alphabet are each about 10%, and about half the fund is in technology.
JHMM: About 700 US mid-sized companies, picked and weighted using several factors such as value, quality and momentum rather than just company size. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
JIRE: Stocks from developed markets outside North America, actively managed by JPMorgan using company research to try to beat the MSCI EAFE index with similar risk. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest at about 3.5%.
JIVE: An actively managed fund of companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US that JPMorgan's team thinks are priced cheaply. Holdings are spread out, with Samsung, HSBC and Taiwan Semiconductor among the largest, each at only a few percent.
JMBS: An actively managed fund of mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged together, mostly backed by US government-linked agencies like Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae. A lot of it is held through to-be-announced (TBA) trades, a way of buying mortgage bonds for future delivery.
JMTG: A manager-run fund of mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans whose payments pass through to investors. It is mostly investment-grade agency mortgage bonds, and no single holding is more than about 2%.
JMUB: An actively managed fund of US municipal bonds, loans to states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It focuses on intermediate maturities and spreads across many issuers and states.
JNK: US dollar corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, called high yield or junk bonds, tracked by a Bloomberg index. They pay more interest than safer bonds but borrowers are more likely to default, and no single bond is above about 1%.
JPIE: An actively managed JPMorgan bond fund that spreads money across mortgage bonds, corporate bonds and other debt, looking for income with limited ups and downs. Government-backed mortgage bonds from Ginnie Mae and Fannie Mae are among its largest holdings.
JPLD: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities (bundles of loans), along with US Treasuries. It keeps its average maturity short, so interest rate changes should affect its price less than a regular bond fund.
JQUA: Large US companies with high quality traits, like strong profits and steady earnings, chosen by a JPMorgan index. It is well spread, with Apple, Microsoft, Broadcom and others each about 2%, and technology is roughly 40% of it.
JTEK: An actively managed fund where JPMorgan's team picks US tech and tech-enabled companies it thinks will keep growing for longer than the market expects. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Intel, Lam Research and Alphabet each about 4% to 5%, and it leans toward chip stocks.
KBWB: Large US banks, tracking the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index, which is weighted by company size with caps on the biggest. It is narrow, all banks, and the top five names (Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo) are around 41% of the fund.
KRE: US regional banks, following an S&P index that holds roughly equal amounts of each. That makes it evenly spread, with each of the biggest holdings about 1%, and it leans more on smaller banks than a typical financial fund.
KWEB: Chinese internet companies, like online shopping, gaming and social media businesses, tracked by an index of such firms. It is concentrated: Tencent, PDD and Alibaba are about 26% of the fund, and Chinese regulation and politics can move it sharply.
LMBS: A manager-run fund mostly in mortgage-related bonds, including those backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, kept short on maturity to limit sensitivity to interest rates. It is spread across many holdings, and the manager has freedom to adjust the mix.
LQD: Bonds issued by large, financially sound US companies (investment grade), tracking the iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate index. It is spread over hundreds of issuers, with no single company above roughly 0.2% of the fund, and it pays regular interest income.
LRGF: Large US stocks picked and weighted toward traits like value, quality and momentum, rather than just by company size. It still looks a lot like the big tech heavy market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it.
LVHI: Stocks of profitable developed-market companies outside the US that pay relatively high dividends and have steadier share prices, following an index built for stable income. It hedges currency back to US dollars and leans toward banks, energy and industrials, with no holding above about 2%.
MAGS: An actively managed fund giving roughly equal exposure to the Magnificent Seven stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, NVIDIA and Tesla. Much of that exposure comes through swaps, contracts that pay the stocks' returns, backed by Treasury bills, so it is a concentrated bet on seven companies.
MBB: Mortgage-backed bonds from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae, which pool home loans and pass the payments to investors, following a Bloomberg index. The government sponsored guarantee makes credit risk low, but homeowners repaying early can change the timing of income.
MCHI: Large and mid-sized Chinese companies, tracking the MSCI China Index, which includes shares listed in Hong Kong, on US exchanges and on mainland China exchanges. Tencent and Alibaba are about 23% of the fund, and it is spread across internet, consumer and bank stocks.
MDY: The original ETF for US mid-sized companies, holding the stocks in the S&P MidCap 400 index in the same proportions as the index. It sits between large and small companies, and no single holding is more than about 1.5% of it.
MGC: Only the very largest US companies, a so-called mega cap group, held in proportion to their size. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 29% of the fund.
MGK: The very biggest US growth companies, following a Morningstar index and weighted by size. It is one of the most concentrated broad funds: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 33% of it, and technology is more than 60%.
MGV: The very largest US companies that look cheap relative to their size, tracking the CRSP US Mega Cap Value index. It leans on financials, health care and technology, with Micron, JPMorgan and Berkshire Hathaway among the biggest holdings at around 3% to 5%.
MINT: Short-term bonds and similar debt, mostly high quality, that PIMCO's managers choose actively to earn a bit more than cash. The prices stay fairly steady because maturities are short, and it holds Treasuries, agency mortgage bonds and corporate debt.
MOAT: US companies that Morningstar believes have lasting competitive advantages, called wide moats, picked when their stock prices look attractive against Morningstar's estimate of value. Holdings are spread out, with the largest only about 3% each.
MSLC: Large US companies chosen from a research based model run by Morgan Stanley, aiming to hold a portfolio close to the broad large company market. NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 16% of it, which is typical of large US stock funds.
MTUM: US large and mid-sized stocks that have been rising the fastest recently, picked and weighted by the MSCI USA Momentum index. It follows recent winners, so it changes often, and Micron, AMD, Broadcom and Intel are among its largest holdings.
MUB: A broad group of US municipal bonds, loans to states, cities and public bodies whose interest is free of federal income tax. It holds thousands of mostly investment grade bonds of medium length, and no single issuer is more than a small slice.
NEAR: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment-grade US dollar bonds, with US Treasuries a large share of it. Because the average maturity is kept short, its price should move less than a regular bond fund when interest rates change.
NLR: Companies tied to uranium and nuclear power, including uranium miners, power producers with nuclear plants and reactor suppliers. Cameco, Constellation, PSEG and BWX Technologies are about 30% of the fund.
NOBL: S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least 25 years, held in roughly equal amounts. No stock is above about 2%, so it avoids the big tech concentration of the S&P 500.
NUDG: An actively managed mix of US dividend-paying stocks, picked for companies expected to keep growing their payouts over time. It looks much like the broad market at the top, with Microsoft, Apple and Broadcom around 19% of the fund, and about a third is technology.
NXUS: Investment grade bonds issued outside the US, from governments, companies and mortgage-style securities in both developed and emerging countries, with currency swings hedged back to US dollars. This keeps results tied mostly to foreign interest rates rather than currency moves.
OEF: The 100 biggest US companies, tracking the S&P 100, which is a smaller version of the S&P 500. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together make up about 31% of the fund.
OMFL: Large US companies chosen and weighted by an index that shifts its mix of size, value and low volatility depending on whether the market is recovering or not. Apple is the biggest holding at roughly 9%, followed by NVIDIA and Alphabet.
ONEQ: Stocks listed on the Nasdaq exchange, tracking the Nasdaq Composite Index and weighted by company size. It is heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon are about 35% of the fund.
PAAA: Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated AAA, the safest slice of bundles of corporate loans packaged into bonds. It is actively managed and floating-rate, so its income moves with short-term interest rates, spread across dozens of issuers.
PAVE: US companies that benefit from building and upgrading roads, rail, power and other infrastructure, including engineering, construction, equipment and materials firms. About three quarters is industrials, with Quanta Services, CSX and Eaton among the top names at roughly 3% to 4% each.
PBUS: Large and mid sized US companies, tracking an MSCI USA index weighted by company size, so bigger firms count for more. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of it.
PDBC: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to widely traded commodities like oil, metals and farm products through futures contracts rather than holding the goods themselves. It is run without a K-1 tax form, and most of the fund sits in cash and short-term securities backing those contracts.
PFF: Preferred stocks, a hybrid of stocks and bonds that pay fixed dividends and get paid before common shareholders if a company struggles. It tracks an ICE index, and these shares are often issued by banks and other financial companies, so income is the main feature.
PGX: Preferred stocks, a hybrid that pays fixed dividends like a bond but trades like a stock, following an ICE index. Big banks such as JPMorgan and Wells Fargo issue many of them, so it leans heavily toward financials.
PPA: US aerospace and defense companies, such as makers of jets, missiles, ships and defense electronics. It is fairly concentrated, with RTX, GE Aerospace, Boeing and Lockheed Martin each making up roughly 7%, and about 90% of it is in industrials.
PRF: About 1,000 of the largest US companies, but weighted by business size such as sales, cash flow, dividends and book value, instead of by stock market value. That makes it less tilted to the biggest names: Apple is about 4% and Alphabet about 4%.
PVAL: An actively managed fund holding a concentrated set of large US companies that managers judge to be priced below their worth. Unlike many value funds it owns big tech: Microsoft and Apple together are about 17% of it.
PYLD: An actively managed PIMCO bond fund that spreads money across many parts of the bond market, such as corporate, mortgage and foreign debt, with managers choosing the mix. It aims to pay steady monthly income and uses derivatives, so its exposure can exceed the fund's size.
PZA: Long term municipal bonds from across the US, tracking an index of bonds whose interest is exempt from federal income tax and not subject to the alternative minimum tax. It holds a very large number of bonds, and none is more than a fraction of a percent.
QLTY: An actively managed fund of US large companies that its manager GMO judges to be high quality, meaning strong, stable profits and sturdy finances. Technology and health care are around 62% of it, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Lam Research are the largest holdings.
QQQ: Tracks the Nasdaq-100: about 100 of the biggest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by size. It is tech-heavy, with technology around 60% of the fund and NVIDIA and Apple together about 14%.
QQQI: The Nasdaq-100 stocks, mostly big tech, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to generate monthly income. The options pay the fund extra cash but cap how much it gains when the market rises sharply.
QQQM: Another fund tracking the Nasdaq-100: about 100 of the biggest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange. Technology is about 60%, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 21%, making it a close twin of QQQ.
QTEC: The tech stocks of the Nasdaq-100, with each company given roughly the same weight rather than by size. That makes it very different from a normal tech fund: small and mid sized chip and software firms matter as much as giants, and no holding is above about 3.5%.
QTUM: Companies tied to quantum computing and machine learning, such as chip makers and equipment firms, held in roughly equal amounts by a Defiance-sponsored index. The biggest holdings are only about 2% each, so it is a spread-out bet on an early, speculative area.
QUAL: Large US companies chosen for quality traits: high profitability, steady earnings and low debt, following an MSCI index. It looks a lot like the broad market at the top, with Microsoft, Apple and NVIDIA about 20% of it, and technology around 41%.
QYLD: The Nasdaq 100 stocks, but with an options strategy called a covered call that sells away much of the future upside in exchange for regular income payments. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 22% of it, and gains are capped in strong markets.
RDVI: US companies with long records of raising dividends, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to bring in extra income. That extra income comes at a cost: it limits how much the fund gains when stocks rise a lot.
RDVY: Large and mid-sized US companies that have raised their dividends and have the cash flow to keep doing so, picked using the Nasdaq US Rising Dividend Achievers index. Despite the income theme, chip equipment makers Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA are its largest holdings at about 13% together.
