RECS: US large and mid-sized companies from the Russell 1000, but chosen and weighted using the manager's research to try to beat the plain index. In practice it is top-heavy: Apple and NVIDIA are each around 11%, and technology is about 39% of the fund.
REET: Real estate investment trusts (companies that own buildings like apartments, warehouses and data centers and pass on rental income) from around the world, tracking a FTSE EPRA Nareit index. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are about 20% of the fund, and most holdings are in the US.
RSP: Holds the same roughly 500 companies as the S&P 500, but gives each about the same weight instead of weighting by size. That means the biggest companies matter far less, and no holding is much above 0.3%.
RSPT: The tech companies of the S&P 500, but each is held in roughly equal amounts instead of by size. That makes it far less top-heavy than most tech funds: the biggest holdings are only about 2% each, and smaller software and hardware firms count as much as giants.
RWL: The companies of the S&P 500, but weighted by their yearly revenue instead of their stock market value. Big sellers like Amazon, Walmart and UnitedHealth get the largest slices, and no company is above about 5%.
SBIL: A government money market fund holding very short term US Treasury bills and similar government securities, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. The price stays steady and the income follows short term interest rates.
SCHA: Small US companies, tracking the small-cap part of the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market index. It holds well over a thousand stocks, so no single holding is large, though Sandisk is the biggest at about 5%.
SCHB: Almost the whole US stock market, around 2,500 of the largest publicly traded companies, weighted by size. Because big companies get the most weight, NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is close to 40%.
SCHC: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, tracking an international small-cap index. It holds many names in tiny slices, with none above about 0.5%, and industrials, materials and financials are the biggest groups.
SCHD: About 100 US companies with long records of paying dividends and solid finances, picked by the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index. Built around steady income, so it leans toward consumer staples, health care, energy and technology rather than the big tech giants.
SCHE: Large and mid sized companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, China and India, tracking the FTSE Emerging Index. It leans on one company: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 17% of the fund.
SCHF: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, covering roughly the top 90% of each market. Financials, technology and industrials lead, and Samsung, SK Hynix and ASML are the biggest holdings at about 2% to 3% each.
SCHG: Large US growth stocks from the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Growth Total Stock Market Index, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 28% of it, and technology is more than half.
SCHH: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties such as apartments, warehouses, data centers and malls, tracking a Dow Jones index that excludes mortgage REITs. Welltower and Prologis are about 19% of it.
SCHI: Investment grade US company bonds maturing in 5 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. They pay more than Treasuries of similar length because companies are riskier borrowers, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 0.3%.
SCHK: The 1,000 largest US companies, held in proportion to their size, covering most of the US stock market by value. It is top-heavy at the top: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of the fund, and technology is around 39% of it.
SCHM: About 500 mid-sized US companies, those ranked 501 to 1,000 by size in the US market, tracking a Dow Jones index. It is spread out: no holding above about 5%, with industrials, technology and financials the largest sectors.
SCHO: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, held all in one portfolio and tracking a Bloomberg index. Backed by the government, and with such short maturities the price moves little when interest rates change.
SCHP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, across a range of maturities from one year up. It tracks a Bloomberg TIPS index, so it holds all those Treasuries and its price still moves with interest rates.
SCHR: US Treasury bonds with roughly 3 to 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index of them. They are backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, but prices still move up and down as interest rates change.
SCHV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their size, tracking the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Value index. It is a mix of financials, technology and health care, with Micron, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan among the biggest holdings at about 3% each.
SCHX: Large US companies from the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Total Stock Market Index, weighted by size. It is much like an S&P 500 fund, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 19% together and technology near 40%.
SCHZ: The broad US investment grade bond market, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, tracking the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 0.4%.
SCZ: Small companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, mainly in Europe, Japan and Australia, tracking the MSCI EAFE Small Cap index. It is very spread out: even the largest holdings are only about 0.4% of the fund each.
SDVY: Small and mid sized US companies with a record of raising their dividends, chosen by a rules-based index. Holdings are spread out, with none above about 1.3%, and it leans away from the largest companies.
SDY: About 100 US companies with the longest records of raising their dividends year after year, tracking the S&P High Yield Dividend Aristocrats index. It tilts toward utilities, consumer staples and financials, and it pays regular income.
SEQ: An actively managed fund holding a small number of companies the manager thinks are undervalued and can grow, from around the world. It is concentrated: Rolls-Royce, Alphabet, Formula One owner Liberty Media and Universal Music are about 35% of it.
SGOL: A fund that holds actual gold bars stored in vaults, so its price follows the price of gold. It owns no stocks or bonds and pays no income, so its value rises and falls with gold alone.
SGOV: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
SHLD: Companies involved in defense technology, such as aircraft, missiles, cybersecurity and military software, from the US and abroad. It is fairly concentrated, with Lockheed Martin, RTX, General Dynamics and Palantir each about 7 to 8%, and Rheinmetall at about 6%.
SHM: Short-term bonds from US states and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, following an ICE index. Short maturities keep price swings small, and no single bond is above about 1%.
SHV: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in under a year, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
SHY: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, tracking an index of those government bonds. Because the maturities are short, its price moves much less than longer bond funds when interest rates change.
SHYG: Short-term US corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (called high yield or junk bonds), limited to those maturing within about five years. They pay higher interest than safer bonds, but the borrowers are more likely to struggle, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
SIL: Companies that mine silver, tracked by a Global X index, so it moves with silver prices and mining costs rather than holding silver itself. It is concentrated: Wheaton Precious Metals, Pan American Silver and Coeur Mining make up almost half of the fund.
SILJ: Smaller silver mining companies, following an index of firms mainly focused on silver. It is concentrated: Hecla, Coeur and First Majestic are about 31% of the fund, so it swings with silver prices.
SIVR: Physically owned bars of silver held in a vault, so the share price follows the price of silver. It holds no stocks or bonds, pays no income, and moves up and down with the silver market.
SJNK: Bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (so they pay higher interest), limited to ones that mature in about one to five years. The short timeline reduces sensitivity to interest rate swings, and holdings are very spread out, with none above about 1% of the fund.
SLV: Physical silver held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of silver. It holds no companies and pays no income, and silver tends to swing in price more than gold because it is also used in industry.
SLYG: Smaller US companies picked from the S&P 600 index because they show faster growth traits, like rising sales and earnings. It holds hundreds of stocks and no single one is much above 1% of the fund, so it is very spread out.
SLYV: Smaller US companies from the S&P 600 index that look cheap compared to their earnings and assets, the 'value' end of small caps. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is much above 1%, so it is spread out across many industries.
SMBS: A broad basket of US mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans guaranteed by government-linked agencies such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. It tracks an index of investment-grade ones, and it is spread across thousands of pieces, so no single holding matters much.
SMH: A concentrated group of the largest semiconductor companies listed on US exchanges, including foreign chipmakers held through depositary receipts. NVIDIA and Taiwan Semiconductor alone are about 27% of the fund, so it rides on a single industry.
SMLF: Small US companies picked and weighted by an index that favors four traits: recent price momentum, high quality, cheap prices and low volatility. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is much above 1%, so it is very spread out.
SMMD: US small and medium sized companies, covering roughly the 2,500 smallest stocks in the Russell 3000 index, weighted by company size. Holdings are spread very thinly across many industries, with individual stocks well under 1% each.
SMTH: An actively managed core bond fund that puts at least 80% in bonds, including government, company and convertible bonds. US Treasuries are among its largest holdings, and the manager can move between bond types.
SOXX: Roughly 30 of the biggest US-listed semiconductor companies, the chip designers and makers, following the PHLX Semiconductor index. It is a narrow, single industry bet: Micron, AMD, NVIDIA, Intel and Broadcom are each roughly 6% to 9%, together about 36% of it.
SPAB: A broad basket of US investment grade bonds, mainly US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, following the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is the kind of core bond fund meant to give steady income, and no single bond is more than about 1% of it.
SPDW: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Japan, the UK, Canada and Europe, weighted by company size. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings, Samsung, SK Hynix and ASML, about 8% together, and financials the largest sector.
SPEM: Large and mid-sized companies from emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India and Brazil, weighted by company size. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 15% of the fund, and technology and financials together make up around half of it.
SPHQ: The 100 stocks in the S&P 500 with the highest quality scores, based on measures like profitability, earnings stability and low debt. It is concentrated, with Mastercard, Visa and Apple together making up about 17% of the fund.
SPHY: High yield bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, tracking a Bloomberg index. They pay more interest because the chance of default is higher, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 0.4%.
SPIB: Investment grade bonds from US companies maturing in roughly 1 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. It pays more than Treasuries because companies are riskier borrowers, and it is spread across many issuers with none above about 0.5%.
SPLV: The 100 stocks from the S&P 500 that have swung the least in price over the past year, so it is built to be steadier than the market. It leans toward utilities, financials and real estate, and no stock is more than about 1.3%.
SPMB: Mortgage-backed bonds from agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which pool home loans and pass the payments to investors. These are backed by government-linked agencies, and the fund holds thousands of these bonds, none more than about 1%.
SPMD: Mid-sized US companies, tracking the S&P MidCap 400 index and holding its stocks in the same proportions. It sits between large and small companies, and no single holding is more than about 1% of the fund.
SPMO: About 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have been rising the fastest over the past year, so it follows recent winners. It is concentrated and changes often: Micron, NVIDIA and Broadcom make up about 27% of the fund.
SPSB: Investment grade bonds from US companies maturing in 1 to 3 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. The short maturities mean smaller price swings, and holdings are spread widely, with none above about 0.6%.
SPSM: About 600 small US companies that are profitable, from the S&P SmallCap 600 index, which requires positive earnings to be included. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and financials, technology and industrials are the biggest sectors.
SPTI: US Treasuries with roughly 3 to 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index. They are backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, though prices still move with interest rates.
SPTL: US Treasury bonds with more than 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index. The long maturities make its price swing more with interest rates than shorter Treasury funds, while credit risk is minimal.
SPTM: The whole US stock market in one fund: large, mid and small companies from the S&P 1500 index, weighted by size. Because big companies weigh most, NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 17% of it.
SPTS: US Treasury notes and bonds that mature in one to three years, so it is a government bond fund with low sensitivity to interest rates. It holds many separate Treasury issues, each only about 1 or 2% of the fund, and income follows short-term rates.
SPY: The first ETF, launched in 1993, and the classic way to own the S&P 500: about 500 of the biggest US companies, weighted by size. It's the most traded fund in the world, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 18% of it.
SPYD: The 80 highest dividend-yielding stocks in the S&P 500, weighted by how much they pay out, so it is built for income. It leans toward real estate, consumer staples, financials and utilities, and each stock is only about 1 or 2% of the fund.
SPYG: The faster-growing companies within the S&P 500, picked by their growth traits and weighted by size. It is heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple together are about 27% of it, and technology is over half the fund.
SPYI: Holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on them to produce extra income. The options cap how much it can gain when the market surges, and as an actively managed fund it is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 18% of it.
SPYM: Another way to own the S&P 500: about 500 large US companies, weighted by size. It holds the same stocks as other S&P 500 funds, so about 40% is technology, with NVIDIA and Apple the biggest names.
SPYV: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, large US companies that score as value stocks on measures like price relative to earnings and book value. Despite the value label, Apple is about 7% of it and technology is the largest sector.
SRLN: Senior loans, which are loans banks make to companies with lower credit ratings, first in line for repayment and with interest rates that float with short-term rates. It is actively managed and aims to beat a leveraged loan index.
STIP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) maturing in five years or less. TIPS have a principal that rises with inflation, and the short maturities mean the price moves less when interest rates change than longer inflation-protected bonds.
SUB: Short-term municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, tracking an ICE index. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the short maturities mean its price moves less than longer muni funds, with no single issuer above about 0.4%.
SUSA: Large US companies from the MSCI USA index, reweighted to favor those with better environmental, social and governance scores while staying close to the overall market. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of it, similar to a regular large company index.
TBIL: A single three-month US Treasury bill, swapped for a fresh one each month, so it acts like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bill is so short and backed by the US government, the price barely moves while income follows short-term rates.
TCAF: An actively managed fund from T. Rowe Price that picks mostly large US companies, aiming for steady growth with less risk. Its biggest holdings are Amazon, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet at about 5% each.
TDIV: Large tech and telecom companies that pay dividends, selected and weighted by a Nasdaq index. Because it focuses on dividend payers rather than growth names, it has older firms like IBM, Broadcom, Microsoft and Texas Instruments, each about 7% to 8%.
TFLO: US Treasury floating rate notes, which are government bonds whose interest payments adjust as short-term rates change. Because of that the price barely moves, and the income rises and falls with short-term interest rates, with a handful of notes making up most of the fund.
THRO: A manager-run fund of US stocks with above-average expected earnings growth, with the manager rotating among market themes. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 23% of it, and technology is around 45% of the fund.
TIP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, with maturities of more than one year. It is one of the oldest TIPS funds, and its price still moves with interest rates as well as inflation.
TLH: US Treasury bonds with 10 to 20 years left before they mature, tracking an ICE index. They are backed by the US government, but with such long lives their prices move noticeably when interest rates change.
TLT: US Treasury bonds with more than 20 years left until they mature. Backed by the government, but because the bonds are so long, the price swings a lot when interest rates move, far more than short-term Treasuries.
TOTL: An actively managed bond fund run by DoubleLine, holding a mix of government, mortgage and company bonds of varying credit quality. It can own up to 25% in riskier high yield bonds, and US Treasuries are among its largest holdings.
TSPA: A US large company stock fund built to look similar to the S&P 500, but with T. Rowe Price's own research team tilting toward the stocks they like. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, close to what a plain index fund would hold.
URA: Companies tied to uranium and nuclear power, including miners, nuclear-related firms and a physical uranium trust, tracking a Solactive index. It is concentrated: Cameco is over 20% of the fund, and the top few names make up around half.
URTH: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries around the world, with the US making up most of it, tracked by an MSCI World index. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 14% of it.
USCA: Large and mid-sized US stocks, weighted toward companies that score better on climate-related measures. It still looks like the broad market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 24% of it.
USFR: US Treasury floating rate notes, government bonds whose interest payments reset regularly with short-term rates. Because the rate resets, its price barely moves and the income rises and falls with short-term rates, with just a few notes making up most of the fund.
USHY: US dollar bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (high yield, sometimes called junk bonds), tracking a broad index of them. They pay more interest than safer bonds because the risk of default is higher, and it spreads across many issuers, with none above about 0.5%.
USIG: A broad basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies with solid credit ratings, from many issuers across industries. It holds hundreds of bonds, none more than a fraction of a percent, and pays regular interest income.
USMC: Roughly the 50 largest US companies, held in proportion to size. It is tilted toward tech: Micron, NVIDIA and Apple together are about 23% of the fund, and technology is around 44% of it, so it is more concentrated than an S&P 500 fund.
USMV: US stocks chosen and weighted to be less jumpy than the overall market, using the MSCI USA Minimum Volatility index. It holds a few hundred stocks spread fairly evenly, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward steadier areas like health care and utilities.
USRT: US real estate investment trusts (companies that own properties like apartments, warehouses and cell towers and pass on rent), tracked by an index that leaves out mortgage REITs. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are about 23% of the fund.
VAW: US materials companies of all sizes, such as chemicals, mining, metals and building materials firms, following a Vanguard-run index. It is top heavy: Linde is about 15% of the fund and Newmont and Freeport-McMoRan add roughly 14% more.
VB: Small US companies, tracked by the CRSP US Small Cap Index and weighted by size. It holds a very large number of names, the biggest only about 0.5%, so it is widely spread across technology, industrials and health care.
VBIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, tracking a Bloomberg index. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, with a price that barely moves and income that follows short-term rates.
VBK: Small US companies with growth traits, following a Morningstar index and weighted by size. It holds hundreds of stocks with none above about 1.3%, leaning toward technology, health care and industrials, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones.
VBR: Small US companies that look cheaply priced, known as value stocks, tracking the CRSP US Small Cap Value Index. It is very spread out, with no holding above 1%, and leans toward financials, industrials and consumer companies.
VCIT: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US and foreign companies, maturing in 5 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. It pays more interest than Treasuries because companies carry more risk, and holdings are spread out, none above about 0.3%.
VCLT: US investment grade corporate bonds that mature in more than 10 years, from a Bloomberg index. Long bonds pay more income but their prices move a lot when interest rates change, and the fund is spread across hundreds of companies.
VCR: US consumer discretionary companies of all sizes, meaning businesses that sell things people want but don't strictly need, like online shopping, cars, restaurants and home improvement. Amazon and Tesla alone are about 42% of the fund, so two stocks drive much of it.
VCRB: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, chosen by a Vanguard team rather than a fixed index. It is very spread out, with the biggest holding only about 1%, and works as a core bond holding.
VCSH: Investment grade US company bonds that mature in one to five years, following a Bloomberg index. Because the bonds are short, the price moves less than with longer bonds, and it holds thousands of issues so no single borrower is more than a tiny share.
VDC: US consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of everyday items like food, drinks and household goods, tracked by a Vanguard index. It is top-heavy: Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola are about 45% of it.
VDE: US energy companies of all sizes, mostly oil and gas producers and pipeline firms, tracking an index of the energy sector. It is very top-heavy: ExxonMobil and Chevron together are over a third of the fund.
VEA: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as those in Europe, Japan and Australia, across large, mid-sized and small companies. It follows the FTSE Developed All Cap ex US Index, and financials, industrials and technology are the biggest sectors.
VEU: Stocks from large and mid-sized companies outside the US, across both developed and emerging markets, tracking the FTSE All-World ex US Index. Financials and technology are the biggest sectors, and Taiwan Semiconductor is the top holding at about 4%.
VFH: US financial companies of all sizes, such as banks, insurers, payment firms and asset managers. It is top-heavy: JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway, Mastercard and Bank of America are about 26% of the fund.
VFLO: About 50 US companies picked for strong free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and investing in it, using a rules-based index. Holdings are spread out, with the largest around 3% each and a mix of energy, software and travel names.
VGIT: US Treasury bonds that mature in about three to ten years, following a Bloomberg index. It is backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, but its price still moves when interest rates change, more than short-term Treasuries.
VGK: Stocks of companies across developed European countries, large, mid-sized and small, weighted by size, following a FTSE index. It holds names like ASML, HSBC, Roche and Nestle, and financials and industrials are the biggest sectors.
VGLT: US Treasury bonds with maturities longer than ten years, tracking a Bloomberg index of long-term Treasuries. Backed by the government, but because the bonds run so long, its price swings much more than short-term bond funds when interest rates move.
VGSH: US Treasury bonds maturing in one to three years, following a Bloomberg index. Backed by the government and short in length, so its price moves very little when interest rates change, and its income tracks short-term rates fairly closely.
VGT: US technology companies of all sizes, such as software, hardware and chip makers, weighted by size. It is extremely top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 41% of the fund.
VHT: US health care companies of all sizes, such as drug makers, insurers, device makers and biotech firms, held roughly in proportion to their size. Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie and UnitedHealth make up about 34% of the fund.
VIG: Large US companies that have raised their dividends steadily for years, rather than the ones paying the highest yields. Broadcom, Apple, Microsoft and JPMorgan are the biggest holdings, and it leans toward technology, financials and health care.
VIGI: Large companies outside the US that have raised their dividends for years, picked by a Vanguard index. It is not heavy in tech, with banks, food and drug makers like Royal Bank of Canada, Nestle and Novartis among the biggest holdings.
VIOO: About 600 small US companies that meet profitability rules, following the S&P SmallCap 600 Index. It holds a lot of names in small amounts, with the biggest each under 1% of the fund, spread across financials, technology and industrials.
VIS: US industrial companies, like aerospace, defense, machinery, airlines and rail, tracked by a Vanguard index. Caterpillar, General Electric and GE Vernova are about 14% of the fund, and it holds large, mid and small firms.
VLUE: Large and mid-sized US stocks that look cheap compared with their earnings, sales and book value, picked and weighted by an MSCI index. It is unusually concentrated for a value fund: Micron is about 19% of it, and technology is over 40%.
VMBS: US government-backed mortgage bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged together and sold to investors, tracking a Bloomberg index of agency mortgage securities. Homeowners' payments flow through as income, and each of the many holdings is a tiny slice, under 1%.
VNLA: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mostly from banks and companies, with a goal of steady income and small price moves. It is spread over many holdings, none above about 1%.
VNQ: US real estate companies, mostly REITs, which own things like apartments, warehouses, data centers and health care buildings. REITs pay out much of their rental income, and Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are among the biggest holdings.
VNQI: Real estate companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging markets, weighted by company size, following an S&P index. It is spread out, with the largest holding, Australia's Goodman Group, only about 4%.
VO: Hundreds of mid-sized US companies, bigger than small caps but smaller than the giants, tracked by the CRSP US Mid Cap Index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
VOE: Mid-sized US companies that look cheap on measures like price relative to earnings or book value, following a CRSP index. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings only about 1% to 2% each, and has more energy, financials and utilities than the broad market.
VONE: About 1,000 of the largest US companies, tracking the Russell 1000 index and weighted by company size, so bigger firms count for more. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together make up about 18% of it.
VONG: Large US companies from the Russell 1000 index that show growth traits, such as fast-rising sales and earnings, weighted by company size. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 34% of it, and technology is well over half.
VONV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, tracking the Russell 1000 Value index. It holds hundreds of stocks, with Micron, Berkshire Hathaway, Alphabet and JPMorgan among the largest at roughly 2% to 3% each.
VOO: The 500 biggest US companies in the S&P 500 index, each weighted by its size. Technology is about 40% of it, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft alone make up close to 18%.
VOOG: The growth half of the S&P 500: large US companies whose earnings and sales are growing faster than average. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet together making up about 36% of the fund.
VOOV: The cheaper half of the S&P 500, meaning large US companies that look inexpensive relative to their size and fundamentals. It still holds big names, with Apple at about 8% and Amazon at about 4%, and spreads across technology, financials, health care and industrials.
VOT: Mid-sized US companies with growth traits, following a CRSP index and weighted by size. Holdings are spread out, with the largest, such as Vertiv and Quanta, around 2% to 3% each, and it leans toward technology and industrials.
VOX: US communication services companies of all sizes, such as social media, streaming, phone and media firms, following a Vanguard sector index. It is very concentrated: Meta and Alphabet (Google's parent, held in two share classes) together make up around 48% of the fund.
VPL: Stocks from developed Pacific countries such as Japan, Australia, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore, weighted by company size. Technology and financials lead, and Samsung and SK Hynix are the two biggest holdings at about 12% combined.
VPU: US electric, gas and water utility companies, held by market size through a Vanguard index. Utilities are known for steady dividends, and NextEra Energy is about 12% of the fund, with Southern Company and Duke Energy next.
VSGX: Large, mid and small companies from developed and emerging markets outside the US, with companies screened out for environmental, social and governance reasons. Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest holding at about 5%, and financials and technology are each about 28%.
VSS: Small companies from developed and emerging countries outside the US, tracking a FTSE index of small caps. It holds thousands of stocks, none above about 0.3%, with industrials, technology and materials the largest sectors.
VT: Stocks from all over the world in one fund, covering the US plus developed and emerging markets, of all sizes, following the FTSE Global All Cap Index. US companies are the biggest share, led by NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft at about 3% to 4% each.
VTEB: A broad basket of US municipal bonds, which are loans to states, cities and public agencies whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It holds thousands of bonds of medium length, and no single issuer is more than a sliver of the fund.
VTEC: Investment-grade bonds from California state and local issuers with medium-term maturities. Their interest is generally free of federal and California income tax, and it is spread over many bonds, none above about 1%.
VTES: Short-term bonds from US states and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. Short maturities keep price swings small, and it is spread over many bonds, none above about 0.3%.
VTHR: The 3,000 biggest US companies, covering about 98% of the US stock market, weighted by size. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is around 38% of the whole fund.
VTI: Nearly the whole US stock market in one fund: thousands of companies of every size, from giants to small firms, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 16% of it, so the biggest names still steer the results.
VTIP: US Treasury bonds that adjust with inflation, known as TIPS, limited to ones maturing in under 5 years. Their value rises with inflation, and the short maturities mean it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than longer bond funds.
VTV: Large US companies that look cheaply priced relative to their size or earnings, known as value stocks, weighted by size. It leans toward financials and health care, with JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway and Johnson & Johnson among the larger holdings.
VTWO: About 2,000 smaller US companies, tracking the Russell 2000 index, which is the standard yardstick for US small caps. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and health care, financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
VUG: Large US companies picked for growth traits, like faster expected sales and earnings growth, weighted by size. It is concentrated, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 32% and technology around 60%.
VV: Large US companies making up roughly the top 85% of the US market by value, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is around 40%.
VWO: Stocks from emerging markets like China, India and Taiwan, tracked by an FTSE index that includes China A shares. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 16% of it, and technology is roughly a third.
VWOB: Bonds issued by governments and government-owned companies in emerging markets, priced in US dollars. They tend to pay more than US government bonds but carry more risk, and the holdings are spread out, with Argentina and Pemex among the largest.
VXF: Everything in the US stock market except the S&P 500: mid-sized and small companies, tracking the S&P Completion Index. It is spread thin, with top holdings around 1% each, and leans toward technology and industrials.
VXUS: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries and of all sizes, following the FTSE Global All Cap ex US Index. Financials and technology are the biggest sectors, and Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest single holding at about 4%.
VYM: Large US companies that pay higher than average dividends, leaving out real estate companies, weighted by size. It leans toward financials, technology and health care, and Broadcom is the biggest holding at about 7%.
VYMI: Stocks of large companies outside the US that pay above-average dividends, in developed and emerging markets, tracking the FTSE All-World ex US High Dividend Yield index. It is spread across many countries and holds banks, drug makers and energy companies, with no holding above about 2%.
XAR: US aerospace and defense companies, tracking an S&P index that holds them in roughly equal amounts rather than by size. That keeps it from being dominated by giants like Boeing: the largest holdings are only about 3% each, and it includes smaller, newer firms.
XBI: US biotech companies from the S&P Biotechnology Select Industry Index, which spreads money across many holdings in nearly equal slices. No single company is more than about 1.5% of the fund, so it is much less top-heavy than most sector funds, but many holdings are small, unprofitable drug developers.
XLB: The materials slice of the S&P 500, such as chemicals, metals and mining, and building materials. It is top-heavy: Linde alone is about 14%, and Newmont, Freeport and Corteva each add around 5% or more.
XLC: The communication services slice of the S&P 500, covering internet platforms, media, entertainment and telecom companies. It is top-heavy: Meta and the two classes of Alphabet stock together make up roughly 43% of the fund.
XLE: The energy companies of the S&P 500, mainly oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline firms, held in roughly the index's proportions. It is very concentrated: ExxonMobil and Chevron are about 39% of it, so those two drive much of the result.
XLF: The financial companies of the S&P 500, such as banks, insurers, payment firms and asset managers, held in roughly the index's proportions. It is fairly concentrated: Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase and Visa alone are about 31% of the fund.
XLG: The 50 largest companies in the S&P 500, held in proportion to their size, so it is a narrower slice of the index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 39% of the fund.
XLI: The industrial companies of the S&P 500, such as aerospace and defense, machinery, transport and electrical equipment makers, held in roughly the index's proportions. Caterpillar, GE and GE Vernova are about 21% of it.
XLK: The technology slice of the S&P 500, holding the index's tech companies in about the same proportions as the index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up around 36% of the fund.
XLP: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: companies that sell everyday essentials like groceries, household goods, drinks and tobacco. Very concentrated: Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola are about 35% of the fund.
XLRE: The real estate slice of the S&P 500, holding the index's property companies such as landlords, cell tower owners and data center operators. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix together are about 27% of it, so a few big names carry a lot of weight.
XLU: The utilities slice of the S&P 500: electric, gas and water companies, plus some power producers. It is steady-leaning and top-heavy, with NextEra, Southern Company and Duke Energy making up about 27% of the fund.
XLV: The health care companies of the S&P 500, including drugmakers, insurers, device makers and hospital operators, in roughly the index's proportions. It is concentrated: Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson alone are about 27% of the fund.
XLY: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: companies selling things people want but do not strictly need, like online retail, cars, restaurants and home improvement. Amazon and Tesla alone make up about 42% of the fund.
XME: Metals and mining companies, including miners of uranium, gold, steel, copper and rare earths, held in roughly equal amounts rather than by size. Because of that, small miners matter as much as big ones, and no holding is above about 5%.
XMHQ: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that score best on quality: high profitability, strong accounting and low debt. It holds a limited set of firms, with the largest each about 3% to 4%, and industrials are about 30% of it.
XMMO: Mid-size US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that have the strongest recent price momentum, meaning they have been rising fastest. The list is reshuffled periodically, so it chases whatever has been working, and it leans toward technology, industrials, health care and energy.
XOP: US oil and gas producers and related energy companies, following an S&P index that gives most stocks similar weight. No holding is above about 3%, so small and mid-sized companies matter as much as the big ones.
XT: Companies around the world working on new technologies, like artificial intelligence, robotics, genomics and cloud computing, picked by an index. Holdings are spread out across many themes and countries, and no single company is above about 4% of the fund.
